item.title: Rockstar Games hasn't said much about who's voicing the GTA 6 cast, but we now know at least one big-name actor attached to the upcoming crime epic: Stephen Root. Read more
item.description:
Rockstar Games hasn't said much about who's voicing the GTA 6 cast, but we now know at least one big-name actor attached to the upcoming crime epic: Stephen Root.
Internet sleuths have been scouring the web ever since the game's very first trailer, searching for even a whiff of the possible GTA 6 cast, and a recurring fan theory is now seemingly confirmed. Asked about the fan speculation by AP News, Stephen Root said, "Yeah, you're gonna see me in that."
You might recognise Root's face from his work in the Oscar-winning horror film Get Out and the Emmy-winning HBO series Barry, but his voice acting career is just as prolific. He has credits in everything from King of the Hill to Rick and Morty, and he even reprised his role as a bubble-loving yellow fish in the Finding Nemo video game.
"It's coming out November 19th, is the latest I know of," said Root. "But, I think, from the first roll out of GTA that they were doing maybe almost a year ago, they had my character in there and there were too many people who knew me from King of the Hill and my voice. So, I think that secret got divulged then."
Root didn't specify which character he's voicing, but fans have long speculated he might be playing Brian Heder. Straight from the horse's mouth, Rockstar's website explains that Brian's a "classic drug runner from the golden age of smuggling" who's "still moving product through his boat yard with his third wife, Lori." You can see Lucia and Jason going out for drinks with Brian and Lori in the GTA 6 extended look.
"I am so happy to be involved with it. It's an amazing thing to look at," added Root.
We'll likely hear more about the character as GTA 6's release date inches ever closer. For now, Rockstar's confirmed there won't be any generative-AI or microtransactions present in the game. GTA 6 is also running at 30 FPS at the moment, with the studio unsure about a possible 60 FPS option.

item.title: Marathon Season 3 and everything that was due to come alongside it has been delayed, including the sci-fi shooter's long-awaited full PvE mode. Bungie's next major update is now launching in December instead, and the famed studio is pivoting away from seasonal updates entirely. Read more
item.description:
Marathon Season 3 and everything that was due to come alongside it has been delayed, including the sci-fi shooter's long-awaited full PvE mode. Bungie's next major update is now launching in December instead, and the famed studio is pivoting away from seasonal updates entirely.
"We previously shared plans for Marathon's next major update to launch on September 22. We know many players were looking forward to it, and we appreciate your patience. We are adjusting our plans to ensure the update meets your expectations," Bungie wrote in a recent blog post. "The content originally planned for September will now arrive as part of our Symbiosis update on December 8."
December's Symbiosis update is promising a new Runner shell, the aforementioned permanent PvE mode, a social space where players can try out weapons together, improvements to the onboarding experience for newcomers, a "refreshed Perimeter zone" and an "experimental" team deathmatch mode.
Rather than a big seasonal feast next week, Marathon players can expect a slightly smaller update on 6 October that'll reset the game's progression and economy, while adding a new Rewards Pass and quality-of-life improvements. Vault Breaker, a different PvE mode that temporarily popped up a few months ago, will also return for a limited time.
From here, Bungie is done with the whole seasonal format, too: "We're also moving away from a strict seasonal schedule. Instead of tying major updates to fixed seasonal deadlines, we're giving the team more flexibility to build, test, and improve features before they are released.
"Since launch, you've told us Marathon needs more depth, more variety, stronger progression, and better reasons to keep playing over the long term. We agree. Addressing that feedback requires us to change both what we're building and how we deliver it," the studio continued.
Bungie's had a tough time both retaining existing Marathon players and courting new ones since the extraction shooter's launch earlier this year. Mass layoffs at the iconic developer - which saw at least 290 jobs cut - likely didn't help matters, either. Here's hoping the Symbiosis update can turn things around.

item.title: Valve has said its new Steam Frame VR headset, despite costing nearly £900 for a base model, is intended to "expand the market" of virtual reality headsets. That's both because it's lightweight and standalone, but also because it addresses a fundamental and long-running problem VR headsets have had. Read more
item.description:
Valve has said its new Steam Frame VR headset, despite costing nearly £900 for a base model, is intended to "expand the market" of virtual reality headsets. That's both because it's lightweight and standalone, but also because it addresses a fundamental and long-running problem VR headsets have had.
"For a long time, VR has turned itself into an accessory for your PC," Valve software engineer Jeremy Selan told Eurogamer in an interview ahead of Steam Frame's pricing announcement, "or in the case even of standalone, something that you have to decide to do first. Like, you might say, 'I want to play a non-VR game on my TV or on my PC,' or, 'I want to go try this specific VR experience.'" Regardless, it's an either-or situation - one or the other.
"From the outset of this product, we were really looking to do something new and to try to make customers not have to think if they wanted to do VR or non-VR games," Selan said. Therefore, a much bigger emphasis has been put on your ability to easily switch between VR and non-VR games - or movies or web browsing - while using the device.
"The non-VR experience is something that I use all the time," Selan went on, "and it's so comfortable because of the ergonomics of the controllers, the lightweightness of the device where you can carry it and use it in a bunch of rooms. So I find myself with this device for the first time putting it on, not even having decided what I'm going to play.
"I have the Steam catalogue in front of me - of course it's your computer and you can install non-Steam games - and I could just say, 'Am I [in the mood for] this non-VR game? Am I in the mood for this VR experience?' And you can sort of jump back and forth. And so this friction of 'am I going to bring out my VR device or not?': if you're already in it, the friction is zero. So I find myself playing a lot more VR and a lot more non-VR simply because of the intermingling of this device."
Matt picked up on this point in his Steam Frame review, and it's these aspects, coupled with its physical design, that make Steam Frame potentially a broader market device, according to Valve. "It's absolutely our goal to expand the market," Selans said.
Valve hardware engineer Joy Lyons added: "The idea here is that we want to have gamers be able to access more content through the Steam store and across all these different systems ... We see this as a product that's growing. This is obviously a great product for our PC VR users, and we love them and support them, this is for them, but we also see this as also a broadening of intent also for developers and then also for gamers just to have more access to more content and a really sort of premium experience in a VR headset."
Nevertheless, a base price of £889 for the 256GB Steam Frame model is a high hurdle to clear - a hurdle Valve's Steam Machine had to contend with earlier this year. The component shortage crisis is largely responsible for Steam Frame's delay from an early 2026 release. "We very much had to adjust the price targets and the volume targets and that's the reality," Selan said. "But we still believe at the current pricing it's a super compelling product. It's a great value. It's an amazing piece of hardware."
Joy Lyons added: "If all hardware is unaffordable then no one is able to enjoy or release or do anything. So, if anything, it's more important to be able to provide equipment that we're really excited about and we think moves forward the gaming experience."

item.title: After years of rumours, and 10 months since its official unveiling, Valve's long-awaited standalone VR headset, Steam Frame, is poised to begin shipping soon, and with a confirmed starting price of £889. Read more
item.description:
After years of rumours, and 10 months since its official unveiling, Valve's long-awaited standalone VR headset, Steam Frame, is poised to begin shipping soon, and with a confirmed starting price of £889.
Frame marks Valve's first VR headset since 2019's Index, and it represents a significant upgrade in almost every regard - from better screens and substantially reduced weight to movement and position tracking that's now handled on-device rather than external base stations.
Its improvements are perhaps less dramatic compared to more modern consumer VR headsets like Meta Quest 3, but they're still notable and you can find full specs on Valve's website. I've been playing with Frame for around two weeks at this point, incidentally, and you'll find more detailed impressions of the device in my Steam Frame review.
The most important bit of today's announcement, then, is probably the price, given Valve's has talked extensively about the tech before. And you'll be able to pick up a Frame with 256GB of storage for £889/€1,049/$1,059 USD (that's around £340 more than a 512GB Quest 3 for some vague comparison), while the 1TB model costs £1,089/€1,279/$1,299. Whichever version you opt for, you get the Steam Frame headset in the box, alongside the attached battery which lives round the back of your head, two controllers, a spacer, a charging cable, and a dongle - which is used for Frame's party trick: the ability to stream games directly from your PC with minimal fuss.
Frame is also being sold alongside a number of first- and third-party optional extras. A PSU from Valve costs £29/€39/$29, and there's an Ergonomic Accessories Kit that's an additional £59/€69/$59 and includes a headstrap, controller handstraps, handstrap battery doors, and an extended light blocker. Also confirmed is a £49/€59/$49 Accessory Replacement Kit, containing a replacement face gasket, head cushion, and light blocker. During an interview with Valve, word of an "enthusiast" accessories pack coming after launch also surfaced. It's said to include a "premium" audio solution and another swappable battery pack, but that's not something Valve's PR has confirmed.
As for Valve's official third-party partnerships, Zennioptical is offering snap-in prescription lenses for around $67.95 a pair, and, if you're not happy with Frame's default monochrome passthrough camera, Arcturus has created a "truly plug-and-play" full-colour camera upgrade for £129/€157/$149.
Once that deadline has passed, Valve will do a "one-time randomisation" to determine reservation and waitlist order. When the process is complete, customers will receive an email on the 17th indicating whether they've made the reservation list or waitlist. Anyone who misses the initial sign-up deadline will automatically be added to the back of the waitlist and be notified once they're moved to the reservation queue.
As to when shipping starts, it's not entirely clear, but Valve says it expects to send the first batch of purchase emails out on 18th September, with more going out as additional units are ready to ship.

item.description:
And so here it is: Steam Frame; Valve's second in-house VR headset following 2019's Index, featuring a boosted spec sheet, PC-to-headset streaming, and the ability to function standalone. It is, if you don't mind spoilers, a good, often great bit of kit, and a fascinating machine - it's lightweight and wonderfully comfortable, with some neat ideas, and it's a pleasure to use if you're doing PC-to-VR. As a standalone device, though, I have reservations, and there's a sense that it's perhaps not quite ready for prime time.
Before we get too far into things, though, a caveat: I love VR, I think it's cool in its niche, and capable of offering a uniquely immersive way to enjoy games (Fireproof's wonderful urban fantasy adventure Ghost Town and Studio Chyr's properly discombobulating room-scale puzzler Hotel Infinity are unquestionably two of my favourite releases of last year). But I'm definitely more of a casual VR fan and not especially technically minded, so if it's a thorough tech breakdown and analysis you're after, Will Judd's Steam Frame preview from last year is a good place to start, followed by RPS hardware editor James Archer's Steam Frame review.
What I can do, though, is whizz through the basics. And compared to Valve's previous foray into VR, 2019's Index, Steam Frame is a huge step up in every way. Its weight has been almost halved, down to 440g from 800g; its screen resolution has been boosted from 1440x1600 per eye to 2160x2160; its display runs between 72Hz and 144Hz, and gone are the old fresnel lenses in favour of pancake lenses, enabling thinner headsets and increased clarity. Movement and position tracking is now handled by on-device cameras rather than separate base stations situated around the room; Frame has an on-device battery so it can be used without being connected to the mains, and, of course, it can operate standalone.
In terms of more modern comparisons, Frame isn't quite as radical an upgrade from 2023's Meta Quest 3 - still one of the most popular consumer VR headsets and a machine I'm more intimately familiar with - but it absolutely brings notable improvements. Per-eye screen resolution is slightly higher than Quest 3's 2064x2208 (but unlike Sony's PSVR2, neither headset features OLED panels), it's slightly lighter (Quest 3 weighs 515g), and it features in-device eyetracking. Elsewhere, Frame contains twice as much internal memory (16GB versus Quest 3's 8GB), and a more performative CPU: the Qualcomm Snapdragon 8 Gen 3 versus Quest 3's Snapdragon XR2 Gen 2 - which should, says RPS' James Archer, be around 30 percent more powerful in synthetic terms, providing a performance advantage over Quest given Frame only has about 2 percent more pixels to push.
So what does all this technology cost? Well, Steam Frame isn't cheap. It starts at £889 for the 256GB model - £340 more than the popular Meta Quest 3, which has 512GB of storage - and climbs to £1,089 if you want 1TB. For that, you get the headset and a swappable battery pack that lives round the back of your head, two controllers, a USB streaming dongle, a charging cable, and a spacer for your glasses - although Valve partner Zennioptical is offering snap-in prescription lenses for around $70 a pair. Then there are the optional upgrades: the £59 Ergonomic Accessories Kit and the separate £29 PSU if you need one.
For some, the £340+ difference between Quest 3 and Frame (likely a result of the AI-fuelled component crisis driving up hardware costs, the better bits inside the Frame, and the fact that, unlike Meta, Valve doesn't subsidise its hardware) won't be factor, particularly if it means they can avoid Meta's Faustian Pact. For others it'll be a far more significant consideration. But whatever you make of the price, my two weeks messing around with Steam Frame have revealed a good bit of hardware with the potential to be great.
Set-up, as you'd hope, is all very simple, aside from an unexpected 40-minute halt as the headset installed its first update - although it's unclear if that's to be expected or just a quirk of the pre-release beta software. And once that's sorted, a number of options immediately present themselves: you can install your games directly to Frame's internal storage for standalone play (Frame supports VR games and flatscreen games via Valve's Proton compatibility layer), or you can stream directly from your PC.
Valve, if you weren't aware, is leaning heavily into Frame's ability to play flatscreen games, which makes a lot of sense: both as a unique selling point, and given the current VR climate which has seen a slowing of VR-focused game releases. And to handle potential compatibility issues, it's implemented a Steam Frame verification system similar to its work with Steam Deck and Steam Machine, meaning everything listed as 'Great on Frame' in your Steam library and in-store should run well in standalone mode. Valve says around 130 games will be Steam Frame verified at launch, but that figure is split between VR games and traditional flatscreen titles (the latter must hit 720p at 30fps and the former must "run at a minimum of 72 fps at 1728x1728" to meet Valve's verification requirements).
And the first big surprise for me after firing Frame up was just how few of the VR games I own currently have Valve's 'verified' seal of approval: Arizona Sunshine 2, Pistol Whip, Moss VR, The Room VR, and Walkabout Golf (my non-VR verified list was far more expansive, including the likes of Factorio, Dread, Inside, Animal Well, Dave the Diver, Silksong, Portal 2, and Streets of Rage 4). Any excuse to play Walkabout Golf is a good excuse in my book, however, and, as expected, its cheery low-poly golfing runs flawlessly in Frame's standalone mode. And the lack of faff required to get it running smoothly provided a handily consistent baseline for testing as I started to get to grips with the Steam Frame hardware itself.
This includes controller grip straps (snugger and more secure than the default Switch-style wrist bands, and enabling you to hold the controllers open-palmed in lieu of handtracking), a sort of rubbery nose flap, and most importantly, a headstrap which provides additional support for Steam Frame, shifting some of its weight from your face. With it installed, I found I could play far longer using the headset, even if it does introduce a few quirks. Chiefly, the strap pulls the top of the headset inward, creating a gap for light to creep in toward the bottom of the goggles, which is where the nose flap comes in. Fitting it is a fascinating adventure, requiring you to pretty much pull the entire headset apart using its clasps and clips - a simple process that provides insight into just how elegantly modular the device is - but once it was in, I did find quite a lot of light could still creep in from below.
As for the headset's picture quality, it's crisp and decently rich, but not, to my eyes at least, an especially notable step up from Quest 3 (I've not used the OLED PSVR2 to compare). It's still quite a 'goggly' headset, too, despite its "up to 110 degrees" field of view. And audio is a touch underwhelming. It utilises "dual speaker drivers per ear, integrated into headstrap", and they're punchy enough, capable of conveying a convincing surround soundscape, but bass leaves something to be desired. And while there's no headphone jack, one of my interviews with Valve mentioned an "enthusiast" accessories pack coming a few months after launch, supposedly including a "premium" audio solution, alongside a swappable battery (right now, you'll get an hour or so of play in standalone mode on a single charge, which isn't great).
Any other quirks? Steam Frame's fan vents circulate a notable amount of cool air around your eyeballs, and eject a surprisingly amount of heat out top - but it's angled in a way that so far hasn't been a concern. Also, I've found it a little tricky to adjust the headset when it's on my face without accidentally dislodging the magnetised strip that holds its cushioning foam in place, requiring a bit of fishing around to recover it. But this stuff is mildly irksome at best, and it's still an extremely comfortable headset I've enjoyed a lot.
One other thing that's worth mentioning: Frame's passthrough cameras, which allow you to see the world outside your headset, are monochrome. Personally, I haven't missed the downgrade from Quest's full-colour cameras given I generally only use pass-through for outside orientation, but if you're a fan of mixed reality gaming it might be a concern. Valve partner Arcturus has, however, created a full-colour camera upgrade for £129/€157/$149, which it claims offers fidelity "beyond" Quest 3 and Apple Vision Pro.
As for Steam Frame's controllers, they're also good! Each weighs around 140g, supports six degrees of rotational freedom, plus full finger and thumb tracking, and you should get around 40 hours on a pair of AA batteries. During play, they feel precise and responsive, and ergonomically, they're very similar to Quest 3's Touch Plus controllers, meaning they sit comfortably and naturally in my average-sized hands, and are lightweight without feeling insubstantial. Notably, though, Frame includes a more generous series of inputs compared to Meta's offering: there's a d-pad on the left controller and four face buttons on the right; each has a control stick, a clicky shoulder button and more resistant trigger beneath it, plus a "dual-stage" inner grip trigger that, if I'm honest, feels a touch too flimsy for my tastes.
But the important bit here: by mirroring the layout of a standard gamepad, pretty much every Proton-compatible flatscreen title you care to throw at Frame should work just fine natively using the included controllers (although you can connect other gamepads, mice, and keyboards via bluetooth if you like). And, actually, I've quite enjoyed Frame's cinema-like wraparound experience while tootling through Cuphead and Hades in standalone mode - and given Frame supports Steam features like cloud saves, it's an easy hop between devices. A minor moan: I'm not a huge fan of the vast circular void Valve still insists on using as a VR backdrop (a couple of cosier options would be nice for flatscreen play), but it does have a few neat tricks. You can, for instance, set the surrounding virtual uplights to mirror what's happening in-game, adding a cute bit of extra immersion while playing.
There's a bit of an important caveat to all this flatscreen talk, though. As nice a feature as it is, especially when there's no guarantee of a regular release cadence for new VR games, Steam Frame isn't a processing powerhouse (it isn't even as powerful as Steam Deck, RPS' James Archer informs me), and that's going to limit what you can play in standalone mode. After a bit of experimentation, 2D games, even those still unverified, seem reliably playable as long as they're supported by Valve's Proton compatibility layer (which essentially allows your Windows games to work on the headset's Linux-based operating system). But when I moved onto modest 3D indies that didn't have Valve's tick, the results were variable. Games like Botany Garden failed to sustain a stable framerate, even on its lowest settings, suggesting most modern blockbusters are out the window unless their dev teams want to roll up sleeves and optimise specifically for Frame. Older-era titles like Dark Souls 2 should work, but even so, I found playing 3D games at 30fps in VR unpleasant enough that I'll likely stick to 2D.
My bigger issue, though, is Frame's standalone VR experience, which feels a little too hit and miss right now. Frame's Proton compatibility layer does a good job of actually getting your games to open, but the results are unpredictable, especially given how comparatively few VR titles are currently verified. Some games I tried work flawlessly out of the box (Walkabout Golf, The Room VR, Pistol Whip, Arizona Sunshine 2), some work well enough with minimal tinkering (Tetris Effect, Ghost Town), others didn't work at all (Serious Sam VR and Escape Simulator refused to boot, The Walking Dead: Saints & Sinners got stuck on the menu, and Myst VR crashed so hard it turned my headset off). Others are absolute slideshows, even on their lowest settings (not that I was expecting much success with No Man's Sky given Frame's standalone limitations), and others are technically playable, but only if you're willing to ditch antialiasing and opt for the lowest resolution.
There's just a little bit too much faff as a standalone experience, and the end results too often feel slightly compromised - it's certainly far removed from the slick plug-and-play of Meta's native games library. Of course, if developers are able to properly optimise their games for the Frame and get that verification tick, the problem should ease with time. But, even so, I can't help feeling verification should be further along than it is right now.
As for the Frame version of Half-Life: Alyx - a game worth mentioning given that it's free with all purchases, and has, according to Valve, shaped so much of Frame's hardware - it's an impressive achievement, making zero concessions in terms of gameplay. Alyx's wonderfully unpredictable mix of blockbuster action and horror, its slick cinematic pacing and clever immersive tricks, still makes for an incredible experience. But there are some compromises you'll have to reckon with. And I found the swirling, shimmering jaggies constantly on the edge of my peripheral vision (it uses foveated rendering to dynamically increase the resolution of whatever you're looking at) just a little too intrusive and distracting.
But! The PC-to-headset experience Valve has cooked up for Frame is a delight, and perhaps the most compelling reason - for me at least - to make the switch from Quest. It all works through Frame's bundled-in dongle, officially a "plug and play 6GHz wireless adapter", that provides an entirely wirefree way of streaming your VR and non-VR games from your PC (but not Steam Machine, at present) to your headset. As someone who has routinely managed to tangle themselves into a wire-based PC-to-VR deathgrip in the past, and who has utterly failed to get Meta's wi-fi reliant Air Link feature working, Valve's solution is elegant and effortless enough to be, for my needs at least, a game changer.
From a tech perspective, as far as I understand at least, the key to it all is foveated streaming - which, in a similar fashion to foveated rendering, uses your eye position to optimise network bandwidth and image quality by decreasing bitrate and pixels outside where you're looking at. And to my eyes, it works extremely well, letting me use the extra grunt of my PC - summoning the added visual bells and whistles, the higher resolution, and refresh rates - while being wire-free, faff-free, and with no obvious degradation in image quality or latency. It's got good range too: I successfully managed to stream to the more room-scale-VR-appropriate office across the hallway from my computer, but your mileage may vary if you don't live in a new-build with paper-thin walls. In fact, the only time the dongle failed was when I ramped up all No Man's Sky's settings, pushing my PC too hard and taking streaming with it.
So that's the Steam Frame. As a standalone machine, I have some reservations: it can be fiddly and unpredictable, far from the plug-and-play ease of Meta Quest, but that's an issue Valve's expanding verification programme will hopefully address over time. But as a PC-to-VR device, it's a delight; liberating in its stress-free, wire-free functionality, if you can deal with the fleeting battery life. And that - alongside the feature bump and wonderfully comfortable headset - has already made Frame my go-to headset, Quest exclusives aside. Frame isn't a machine for high-end enthusiasts though, I don't think, and despite its many nice-to-haves, it perhaps doesn't offer a dramatically different in-headset experience to the far cheaper, more intuitive Quest 3, meaning Meta's machine is still in the conversation. And so, honestly, I'm not sure if the Frame is for you. But as unhelpful as this might be, if you think it is, you're probably right.
A Steam Frame was provided for this review by Valve.

item.title: Netflix is binge-producing video game adaptations faster than a certain Blue Blur can chow down a chilli dog. The streamer has just announced a new partnership with Sega to make another animated TV show based on Sonic the Hedgehog, as well as films adapting Crazy Taxi and the upcoming Stranger Than Heaven. item.description:
Netflix is binge-producing video game adaptations faster than a certain Blue Blur can chow down a chilli dog. The streamer has just announced a new partnership with Sega to make another animated TV show based on Sonic the Hedgehog, as well as films adapting Crazy Taxi and the upcoming Stranger Than Heaven.
The multi-project deal supposedly begins with a feature-film adaptation of Crazy Taxi, Sega's long-running series of whacky arcade racing games that's being revived soon, penned by the screenwriting duo responsible for last year's The Naked Gun reboot (Dan Gregor and Doug Mand). The producers behind the surprisingly good live-action Sonic films (Neal H. Moritz, Toby Ascher, and Sega's Toru Nakahara) are also involved with this one, per Variety. No telling if it'll be animated or live-action, though.
On the flip side, the Sonic Netflix series is set to be an animated romp that, according to Sega, is "high-voltage, comedic, yet emotionally grounded" and is "built for kids who want to feel a little edge, a little attitude, and a lot of 'that's my crew' wish fulfillment." Expect to see lots of the extended anthropomorphic Sonic family, then. Nakahara and animation director Carlos Stevens are attached.
And, finally, we have a film adaptation of Stranger Than Heaven also planned. RGG Studio's crime-ridden action game isn't due to come out until next year, 15 January, but Sega's giving it the multimedia treatment early.
"Expect something cute yet cool for Sonic, hilariously crazy for Crazy Taxi and a badass action drama for Stranger Than Heaven, because we've got some amazing creative ideas lined up and we are just getting started," Nakahara said in a statement to Variety.
Netflix has already scooped up the rights to plenty of big name video games (Castlevania, Cyberpunk, Devil May Cry, Arcane, more) and has plans to turn a bunch more into streamable hits (including Gears of War, Assassin's Creed, Crash Bandicoot and - shudders - Persona).

item.description:
Did you enjoy Lies of P? The game - a Soulslike take on the story of Geppetto and Pinocchio - was very succesful when it launched in 2023. Now, it looks like we may have our first proper glimpse at what the game's sequel may turn out to be. A couple of new trademarks have appeared over at the European Union Intellectual Property Office (EUIPO), registered by publisher Neowiz, for a mysterious project called 'Wonders of O'.
Tags included in the IP notice include "interactive multimedia software for playing games; computer software for use in providing multiple user access to a global computer information network; computer game software downloadable from a global computer network and wireless devices; computer game software downloadable from a global computer network" and so on, so it's safe to say we are looking at the registration of a video game here. Additionally, Neowiz is the owner of the application. All signs point to this being a sequel.
In terms of the name, you don't need to be a detective to work out the naming pattern there, do you? I wonder what the 'O' could refer to. Oz, perhaps - from The Oz books that form a book series that begins with The Wonderful Wizard of Oz (1900), by L. Frank Baum. There are 14 books in the Oz canon, so there will certainly be plenty to draw from there, if that's where the Korean developers choose to go with the sequel. Will it be connected to Lies of P at all, or just a standalone project? It remains to be seen. It's also worth noting that the post-credits scene of the first game seemed to feature Dorothy - heroine of the first few Oz books. Go figure.
It's not actually the first time we've heard about this game. Just after the first title released, the developer(s) confirmed a sequel is in the works. Then, back in August, a Lies of P documentary teased that the next game "is going to be really fun and emotionally moving", indicating a bit more ambition from the studios behind the title compared to the relatively narrative-light original game. The documentary also revealed a bit about the studio's philosophy: one internal team at Round8, known as Nough, is dedicated to "testing and refining" its projects before its release, and proudly proclaims it makes "games by gamers".
"We're giving it everything we have to make it the best it can be. So please, just wait a little longer," noted director Choi Jiwon in the documentary. "You won't be disappointed, we promise. This is the truth, not a lie." Very fitting for the Pinocchio-themed game.
Eurogamer's three-star review of 2023's Lies of P said it has "strong enough foundations in its edgy tone and tweaked weapons", but "it's highly unlikely that they'll be able to beat the originals at their own game".
Stay tuned for more information soon. A Game Awards reveal, perhaps? We'll see.

item.title: Blizzard has revealed more tangible details about what the new StarCraft game actually is, beyond it being an open-world shooter due for release in 2030. In doing so, Blizzard likened it to being more of a 'boxed' release rather than an ongoing live-service game, which is a notable departure for a company that has dealt almost exclusively in online multiplayer games. item.description:
Blizzard has revealed more tangible details about what the new StarCraft game actually is, beyond it being an open-world shooter due for release in 2030. In doing so, Blizzard likened it to being more of a 'boxed' release rather than an ongoing live-service game, which is a notable departure for a company that has dealt almost exclusively in online multiplayer games.
"If I were to describe the overall structure we currently envision, it's a 'box product'," project leader Dan Hay said during a Korean media roundtable at BlizzCon 2026, reported by Inven Global. "It is a narrative-driven open-world shooter where players create a character, name them, and follow that character's story. The story has a beginning, a middle, and an end.
"You can roam around and explore a rich open world, but our story has a definitive ending. Think of it as purchasing a standalone boxed game, playing it, and experiencing its story. We hope players enjoy it, love it, and return to us later. At the very least, what we are building right now is not a seasonal game."
Dan Hay oversaw the Far Cry series at Ubisoft for 10 years, from Far Cry 3 to Far Cry 6, so he comes from a much more traditional "boxed" game background. When describing the game's structure, Hay said StarCraft has a mix of focused story-based missions set within a wider open-world, which put me in mind of the open zones in Doom: The Dark Ages, that you can return to between more focused story-based levels.
"The shooter we are building features a deep story, main missions, side quests, and character progression," Dan Hay said. "While it will be a gritty and challenging game, we aren't trying to make it overly punishing. We want to present a degree of challenge while letting players experience an adventure within it. In particular, if a certain mission feels too difficult, you can return to the open world and engage in other activities at your own pace."
One part of StarCraft is "serious missions" that have "a powerful narrative" running through them, then. Hay used the moment Kerrigan was abandoned in StarCraft as an example of the "intensity of emotion" he wants these missions to deliver.
"Conversely," he added, "in the open world, players can progress at their own speed. If you lack adequate gear, you can head out into the world, scavenge for what you need, deck out your armour, and try again. We chose a narrative-driven game to give players the time and space to experience the world at their own pace. Tackling intense missions, and then, if needed, stepping back out into the free open world to play your own way - that is the game we are making."
Hay wants this game to feel "very up-close and personal", as though you're witnessing a StarCraft battle at eye height from the middle of it. Tonally, Hay loves "the gritty, rough edge unique to StarCraft" and its "space Western sensibility". "It has that vibe of being on the frontier - remote, distant, and isolated". "The characters aren't people who always just do what they're supposed to do, either. In fact, they often do things they shouldn't," he said.
The story itself takes place 70 years after previous events in the StarCraft series, which I assume means after StarCraft 2: Legacy of the Void and DLC Nova Covert Ops. Much has changed. There are "countless political moves taking place between hostile forces, with factions constantly clashing", which sounds like an ideal set-up for an open-world you can make differing alliances in.
Speaking of which, the famous Protoss faction is there, Hay confirmed, it's just not super-visible in the debut StarCraft trailer (perhaps because of its cloaking tech). "There's an underlying tension that the whole world could tilt into catastrophe at any moment," Hay added. "That's why I feel it's vital for StarCraft to maintain that dark and gritty atmosphere."
But the existence of a StarCraft shooter rather than an RTS does throw doubt over the future of the series, and whether Blizzard intends to develop this way or whether it has, additionally, plans for an RTS at any point. Addressing this, Hay said: "That's a very big and important question.
"First off, the starting point for developing this title as an open-world game was the story. There was a narrative we wanted to tell, and development began from figuring out how to realise that vision. However, I have to be extremely careful when answering what we might do in the future."
Blizzard is aware of the "hugely important and powerful position" StarCraft holds as an RTS, and it's always thinking about the future. "I'm always pondering where we can go next and what we can do in the future," Hay said. "But I want to avoid a situation where I say something here and headlines come out reading 'Blizzard Developing Another StarCraft Game Beyond This Title'. I know how important this question is, but I cannot speak beyond that today."
Blizzard's StarCraft announcement - and it's surprisingly far-off date of 2030 - was one of a few big reveals during the BlizzCon 2026 Opening Ceremony. We also got the surprise announcement of Diablo 5, the World of Warcraft Forever (Classic Plus) reveal, a new Warcraft 3 RTS campaign, and more besides. It was a busy weekend.

item.title: The announcement of Diablo 5 at BlizzCon over the weekend was among the fan event's highlights. Blizzard shared a surprising number of details about a game that's early in development, and one that won't be released for another three years. Read more
item.description:
The announcement of Diablo 5 at BlizzCon over the weekend was among the fan event's highlights. Blizzard shared a surprising number of details about a game that's early in development, and one that won't be released for another three years.
Comparisons to Diablo 4 are inevitable, of course, but they're especially relevant considering how different Diablo 4 is to what came before - Diablo 4 is essentially an ARPG wrapped in an MMO skin.
So can we expect Diablo 5 to follow Diablo 4's example? Blizzard is being coy. Senior game director Joe Shely revealed in a group interview at BlizzCon (via PC Gamer) that Diablo 5 will indeed support multiplayer, just like it will be playable solo.
"Like Diablo 4, it is a game that you can play solo or multiplayer, however you please, and you should be able to play all of the content with your friends," said Joe Shely.
As far as the structure of the multiplayer experience, Blizzard said those details will be confirmed closer to Diablo 5's 2029 launch. How the game handles multiplayer and co-op is a notable topic here because of a major returning feature: the game's procedurally-generated world.
As confirmed during BlizzCon, Diablo 5 is bringing back Diablo 3's procedural generation tech, which randomises the layouts of dungeons each time you enter. The same is also true for the overworld, with Blizzard emphasising that regions will be altered on every visit.
In other words, each player could technically experience a different version of Sanctuary. That decision may make it difficult for Diablo 5 to borrow Diablo 4's MMO-lite approach to multiplayer, but we're only speculating here.
It's also worth pointing out that Diablo 5 isn't bringing back towns, which, among other things, act as hubs for players to meet and rest up in between quests. Diablo 5 instead tells the story of a caravan of lone survivors on the road across Sanctuary, so finding ways to interact with other players may prove challenging.
Blizzard promised to start sharing regular Diablo 5 development updates sometime in 2027. Indeed, the developer said it's open to feedback, so some of what's revealed may look different come launch.

item.title: Blizzard uncharacteristically announced two games at the weekend with release dates surprisingly far away. One was Diablo 5, which Blizzard plans to release in spring 2029, and the other was the much-rumoured StarCraft open-world shooter, releasing 2030. Read more
item.description:
Blizzard uncharacteristically announced two games at the weekend with release dates surprisingly far away. One was Diablo 5, which Blizzard plans to release in spring 2029, and the other was the much-rumoured StarCraft open-world shooter, releasing 2030.
The dates caused commotion. There was more than a decade between the releases of Diablos 2 and 3, but there will be only six years between 4 and 5 (which has caused concern about whether there will be any more Diablo 4 expansions). And StarCraft in 2030? I can't think of any studio dating games further away than 2028, let alone Blizzard, which famously has operated with a 'done when it's done' kind of approach, keeping dates obscured to the last moment.
It's a way of doing things that, for Blizzard, is unprecedented, and it begs the question of why do it at all. "We want to convey confidence in some of our biggest bets coming forward," answered Blizzard president Johanna Faries, speaking to Bloomberg in an interview. "We're a Blizzard that's going to ship, and ship big, and ship on time, and all hands on deck to set those projects up for success."
One explanation for the change of approach could come from looming Xbox layoffs. Microsoft cut 1600 people from the Xbox division earlier this year but still has 1600 more cuts to make between now and next summer. Does shouting about these big projects - Blizzard also announced the ambitious World of Warcraft: Forever, to launch in November - underline the company's importance and in some way shield it from Microsoft's scissors?
Not a lot was revealed about the StarCraft shooter at the weekend, though we've learned more about it since. Former Ubisoft Far Cry overseer Dan Hay came on stage to reveal it - who was reported to be working on the game in 2024 - and told us the game would be open-world and tonally on the serious side. A CGI trailer showed Terran mech-pilot recruits training and going to war, then dying in zerg stampedes, before their mech suits were returned and cleaned of pulped body-sludge for the next round of recruits to occupy. The message was their lives didn't matter and chances of survival were slim - will you fare better?
A shooter is a notable departure for StarCraft, which is known as an RTS series, though there was a failed attempt to make a StarCraft Ghost stealth-like shooter many years ago. Faries called the new StarCraft a "broadening" of the series and labelled it "a StarCraft for the modern, next generation of players without departing from our RTS roots", which is a curious thing to say - does that suggest it has RTS elements to it? "We'll have more to say about that, you know, over the years here," Faries added. The intention of revealing it so early was "starting a new conversation around it".
Besides Diablo 5, the StarCraft shooter, and World of Warcraft Forever, Blizzard also announced a Diablo Netflix animated series - alongside broader plans to do similar with many of its brands - a brand new Warcraft 3 campaign decades after the game's release, a new Overwatch hero (and tease of what to expect in next year's big expansion-like release), a new Diablo 4 class, and outlined the next big patch for World of Warcraft's Midnight era. It was a big show, and you can catch up with our blow-by-blow account of the BlizzCon 2026 Opening Ceremony elsewhere on the site.

item.title: Development on a multiplayer PvP mod for The Last of Us Part 2 on PC has been halted after PlayStation got in touch and asked the developers to cease work on the project. Read more
item.description:
Development on a multiplayer PvP mod for The Last of Us Part 2 on PC has been halted after PlayStation got in touch and asked the developers to cease work on the project.
"Hey everyone, as you all know, the [The Last of Us Part 2] multiplayer mod that has been in development since January was supposed to [be released] this month," wrote modder Speclizer in a post on social media. "Unfortunately I recently received a letter on behalf of Sony Interactive Entertainment requesting for the mod not to be released. Extremely sad that this never got to see the light of day but I hope you'll continue to follow me onto the next project, this time something of my own."
If you were curious about what the mod what have looked like in action, Speclizer uploaded about 25 minutes of gameplay for the mod back in June. You can see the video below. Given that the team has spent nine months working on the project, the legal request from Sony no doubt stings - but what did PlayStation's legal team seek out cancellation of this mods when there are so many others out there? It may be because the team behind this one would have added a paid component to the mod, funded by a Patreon account - something that tends to get unofficial mods shut down.
The mod would have been quite an extensive one: the final project promised to include listening mechanics to help you figure out where enemy players were, different perks that would help you out in various ways, and a suite of maps that we didn't see in the base, single-player game.
I imagine this news is going to sting for anyone that was particularly miffed about The Last of Us Online getting cancelled, which we learned about in 2023. That project was reportedly 80 percent complete by the time it was culled, and had a loyal early base of players. Between that, and the popularity of this sadly-cancelled mod, there is clearly an appetite for Last of Us multiplayer experiences, though whether that's something Sony will pursue feels dubious at this point.
If you've never played the multiplayer mode in the original The Last of Us, it was a pretty unique mode that highlighted the stealth gameplay of the series and turned it into a more tense, emergent experience.

item.title: One of the biggest questions that emerged following the surprise reveal of Diablo 5 at BlizzCon over the weekend surrounded the future of Diablo 4. Blizzard announced a returning class - the Amazon - coming to the game sometime in the first half of 2027, but nothing beyond that. Read more
item.description:
One of the biggest questions that emerged following the surprise reveal of Diablo 5 at BlizzCon over the weekend surrounded the future of Diablo 4. Blizzard announced a returning class - the Amazon - coming to the game sometime in the first half of 2027, but nothing beyond that.
Of course, the question on everyone's mind was whether the game will be getting any more expansions in the three-year wait between now and the 2029 release of Diablo 5. The studio's answer will likely disappoint many.
"We're all focused on [Diablo 4] seasons and getting to Diablo 5," Diablo game director Brent Gibson told PC Gamer. "We feel like we told the Story of Hatred. We had a great conclusion with Lord of Hatred with what we have with Mephisto, and we are moving towards telling the Story of Terror."
Lord of Hatred indeed had a great sense of finality, but I am willing to bet many simply saw it as the end of one arc rather than the game's entire story. Speaking of which, more story content is coming, but it will be delivered through upcoming seasons.
The events of Diablo 5 take place a century after Diablo 4 in a completely changed Sanctuary. It would have been nice to have a major Diablo 4 expansion serve as a narrative lead-in, but perhaps the 100-year gap is large enough to make that difficult. Still, Blizzard wants to do some of that work with seasonal content, but the developer doesn't quite know what shape things will take just yet.
"So continuity is something that we're really excited about, but we don't necessarily have a perfect picture on exactly where that's going to go because we want to see how fans are reacting season to season," Gibson added.
In the more immediate term, Diablo 4's next season - Season of Hell's Legacy - kicks off tomorrow, 15th September. The season is a celebration of the franchise's 30th anniversary, bringing back Deckard Cain to aid the player in a quest where they face all three original Prime Evils: Diablo, Baal, and Mephisto. The same day also sees the release of the long-rumoured Switch 2 port, which includes all previously-released content.

item.title: Level-5 president and CEO Akihiro Hino has confirmed that generative AI was used in the studio's recent showcase. Read more
item.description:
Level-5 president and CEO Akihiro Hino has confirmed that generative AI was used in the studio's recent showcase.
As spotted by VGC, fans quickly called out suspected undisclosed AI after the studio's digital showcase debuted last week.
Now, in response to the backlash, Hino has confirmed AI was used to make the presentation footage "more spectacular", admitting: "It appears that some people felt uncomfortable about this, so I deeply apologise".
1日違いの公式トレーラーですら顔が変わる品質で「AI使って効率化してるんです！」とか笑えるな効率化した結果がこれかよ pic.twitter.com/3xWeg8M08J
"I was SO excited when Level-5 announced their big comeback with Professor Layton, Decapolice, Yo-Kai Watch, and more," wrote one fan on X/Twitter. "But seeing this much blatant genAI being used across their games… yeah, this ain't it."
"This time, because we used AI for the footage within the event, it seems that concerns have arisen regarding the content of the works as well, so I would like to provide an explanation," Hino said on X/Twitter (as translated by machine).
"It was entirely due to the desire to make the presentation more spectacular that we incorporated processing that also served as an experiment using the latest AI. It appears that some people felt uncomfortable about this, so I deeply apologise."
【AIの使用について・LEVEL５VISION2026Ⅱ】今回、イベント内のでの映像についてAIを使用したため…
"However, at our company, the parts that relate to the charm and individuality of the released works - such as scenarios, character designs, and basic settings - are all created by human hands," he insisted.
"What we're aiming for in terms of efficiency through AI is mainly the digitisation of creative work made by people, for example, accurately converting original artwork into polygons and such. Please rest assured that no simplistic AI-generated output data is included in the games that are released."
He also claimed Level-5 used AI as "trial and error" as part of its commitment to slicing development time from five years down to two.
"That said, it's undeniable that this time, out of the desire to create a clear and flashy presentation, we ended up using AI in a wide variety of ways," he said. "We will take this as a lesson and carry it forward to the next one, so please look forward to Level Five's next presentation."
Level-5 is not alone, of course - many other game companies, including Krafton, Square Enix, EA, and more, have invested heavily in AI tech.

item.title: Diablo 4's next season, Season of Hell's Legacy, will go live on 15th September to celebrate the franchise's 30th anniversary and Nintendo Switch 2 debut. Read more
item.description:
Diablo 4's next season, Season of Hell's Legacy, will go live on 15th September to celebrate the franchise's 30th anniversary and Nintendo Switch 2 debut.
At BlizzCon's opening ceremony, developer Blizzard said the season will be a tribute to three decades of Diablo, built around the return of Deckard Cain and a rematch against all three original Prime Evils: Diablo, Baal, and Mephisto.
Cain's spirit returns to warn players that echoes of the three Prime Evils have resurfaced. Each one's holed up in a location familiar to those who've played the earlier games - Tristram Cathedral, Arreat Summit, the Durance of Hate. Beat one and you get a Soul Splinter, which lets you borrow a bit of that demon's power. The catch is that it also makes you more vulnerable to that same demon.
That's not all, either. Nine new Legacy Uniques also join the game permanently, including a returning Stone of Jordan, alongside a batch of enemy encounters called Waking Nightmares that recreate specific moments from Diablo's past.
The new content is slated to go live at 5.30pm UK time on 15th September.
Diablo 4 is also making its Nintendo Switch 2 debut that day. The Age of Hatred Collection brings the base game with the Vessel of Hatred and Lord of Hatred expansions, supporting cross-play and cross-progression with other versions.
The Amazon's back too, marking her first appearance in Diablo 4. She's due sometime in the first half of 2027, with a bow and javelin in hand and four builds: Champion, Skirmisher, Ranger, Commander.
It's one of several big reveals from BlizzCon 2026's opening ceremony, which also included Diablo 5, World of Warcraft: Forever, and a new open-world StarCraft shooter. For more, here's everything announced in the BlizzCon 2026 Opening Ceremony.

item.title: Blizzard has officially confirmed World of Warcraft: Forever, the long-rumoured "Classic+" experience. Read more
item.description:
Blizzard has officially confirmed World of Warcraft: Forever, the long-rumoured "Classic+" experience.
Last week, World of Warcraft fans were obsessing over colours as dataminers pulled hues from Blizzard's website that were labelled under a curious "wow 2" tag, leading many to speculate that this referred to the rumoured World of Warcraft Camelot, or as it's better known, "Classic Plus", much like how Blizzard is now expanding Diablo 2.
Now, following BlizzCon's opening ceremony, it turns out the rumours were pretty much bang on and World of Warcraft: Forever launches globally on 4th November.
If November sounds very far away, worry not; beta access begins this Thursday, 17th September, for anyone who's pre-purchased one of the game's upgrade packs.
A dedicated panel featuring senior game director Ion Hazzikostas, lead Classic designer Tim Jones, lead software engineer Nora Mills, and associate production director Clay Stone went into more detail on the new regions, systems, and design philosophy behind the project.
Blizzard describes Forever as a new permanent home for WoW alongside Modern and Classic rather than replacing them. It takes place between two fixed points in WoW lore - after the new Forsaken Kingdom campaign, but before the original Molten Core raid. Players will head back to the original continents with a level cap of 60.
WoW Forever will boast three new zones from launch, along with more than 1,000 new quests, nine new dungeons, two new raids supporting both 10 and 20-player groups, new race and classes, and a brand new playable race called the Skyborne.
Best of all, no separate purchase is required, as access is included with an existing WoW subscription. That said, optional upgrade packs can be bought separately, such as the Skyborne Heroic Pack, which unlocks the Skyborne race and a starting zone early. The pricier Skyborne Epic Pack gives beta access, a month of Game Time, and additional cosmetics.
It's one of several big reveals from BlizzCon 2026's opening ceremony, which also included Diablo 5 and a new open-world StarCraft shooter. For more, here's everything announced in the BlizzCon 2026 Opening Ceremony.

item.title: Blizzard's next StarCraft game will be an original open-world shooter and it's coming spring 2030. Read more
item.description:
Blizzard's next StarCraft game will be an original open-world shooter and it's coming spring 2030.
Revealed at BlizzCon 2026's opening ceremony, it marks the first new standalone StarCraft game in around a decade.
Dan Hay, who previously worked as lead producer on Ubisoft's Far Cry series before joining Blizzard, introduced the project, calling it "something new - an open-world shooter where every step is earned. Not from above, but down on the ground, in the mud, in the fire".
"There's only one thing we can say: it's about damn time," Blizzard teases on its website.
The announcement was accompanied by a brilliantly grim cinematic teaser rather than gameplay, following a Terran recruit called Holt whose deployment ends violently within moments of touching down on the Zerg-infested battlefield. Though not confirmed, it sounds as though Arcturus Mengsk is broadcasting throughout the trailer.
"The sons and daughters of the Dominion answered the call when mankind needed them most. Their courage held the line. Their sacrifice bought us another day. Now the call comes to you. Carry their strength forward. No matter the cost," says the description accompanying the three-minute trailer.
Beyond that details are thin, although interestingly, only an Xbox logo is on the "returns 2030" screen, suggesting Xbox is sticking to its word of keeping its biggest games Xbox-exclusive.
In the same opening ceremony, of course, we learned about Diablo 5, the next mainline entry in the series expected to arrive in spring 2029, and confirmation that an animated Diablo series is in development at Netflix. For more, here's everything announced in the BlizzCon 2026 Opening Ceremony.

item.title: Blizzard has officially announced Diablo 5, confirming the next mainline entry in the series is expected to arrive in spring 2029. Read more
item.description:
Blizzard has officially announced Diablo 5, confirming the next mainline entry in the series is expected to arrive in spring 2029.
Announced during BlizzCon 2026's opening ceremony, Blizzard has flipped the franchise's usual setup, as every prior Diablo game has centred on stopping an apocalypse before it happens, and this one starts after one is already underway.
According to Blizzard, Diablo 5 is set a century after the events of Diablo 4, in a Sanctuary where Diablo has already triumphed and its heroes have already been defeated: "Sanctuary has fallen. Diablo won".
A panel, hosted by Blizzard president Johanna Faries alongside the Diablo 5 development team, offered an early look at the game's world, classes, and creative direction. It confirmed two returning classes - Demon Hunter and Monk - alongside brand new class Plague Knight.
Beyond that, details were scarce, and we didn't get any insights into core gameplay systems, progression, or how any of this will actually translate into play.
Blizzard also confirmed that a Diablo animated series is in development with Netflix, though I'm afraid we didn't get many details about that, either.
"Sanctuary's darkness is spreading," the description teases. "Blizzard and Netflix are developing a new animated series set in the world of Diablo, bringing the franchise to a new screen. We'll have more to share as the series takes shape. Until then, stay awhile... and stay tuned."
The Diablo franchise has passed more than 130 million players worldwide since its original 1996 release, and this year marks its 30th anniversary.
For more, here's everything announced in the BlizzCon 2026 Opening Ceremony.

item.description:
Going through Miles Buckle's Instagram feed is like stumbling into a parallel universe where cinema's greats – Lynch, Hitchcock, Fellini, Kubrick – are reimagined in the familiar but distinctly different visual language of video games. The "here's Johnny" scene from The Shining, where Jack Nicholson terrorises Shelley Duvall, recreated in the stilted comedic style of The Sims 2. The opening sequence of Twin Peaks told through the landscapes of SimCity 2000 – one of several "orthographic experiments" that Buckle has done using the most iconic Maxis game of my childhood. A low-poly Peter Finch doing the Oscar-winning "I'm a human being, god dammit!" monologue from Sidney Lumet's classic Network. Perfect fever dreams that can't and won't exist outside of these short clips.
As a twelve-year-old, Buckle soaked up Minecraft animations and parody songs on the internet, and posted his own Minecraft art experiments on YouTube. "I remember a family friend showed me Blender, I don't know quite what they were using it for, but I quite quickly got obsessed with the idea of being able to make something genuinely without limits," Buckle says. "Things like Lego or Minecraft… they're very creative for building. But… you're confined by the bounds of what the thing is meant to look like, especially with Lego. You're also then confined by what you actually own." Through the holy trinity of Lego, Minecraft, and Blender, his journey toward 3D art was purely about wanting to make things the way he wanted them to look. But what really set him down the low-poly path was, unsurprisingly, a Twin Peaks fangame demo on itch.io, Into the Night, which was removed after the copyright banhammer came down.
For his university degree show last year, Buckle, who studied graphic communication design at Central St. Martin's in London, showed his final project, a short game called Nights Bridge, on a plastic-molded cream-griege desktop computer from the ancient times. "I bought a PC from the 90s off eBay," the 3D artist and animator tells me on a video call. "I took the parts out and put in modern hardware, so the monitor and the tower were like, 30 years old, and it had the keyboard and everything." He remembers all of it being obstinately heavy – it was a click-and-collect pickup situation, and he hauled it all home on foot.
Most of the other students in the programme were focused on things like typography and bookmaking, and Buckle recalls that while the project was received well at the degree show, most people were interested in the technical side of his project rather than the concept. Nights Bridge was an interactive narrative work exploring the nature of memory and graphic fidelity – a fleshed-out version of an earlier project. Buckle describes a mundane setting based on chores – "you're cooking, you can have a bath, you can collect your post and stuff," he says – the experience of existing in a world, being bored, before you start noticing odd little things happening around you.
"When you remember something, especially from your childhood, you remember it in a really specific way. It's not necessarily how it actually happened… and I was attaching that idea to graphical fidelity," Buckle says. "So I had the present, which was quite hyper-realistic, and then you go back a few years and it was kind of PS1 graphics, then you'd go back even further and it was like Mario side-scroller. As the fidelity of the memory got worse, so did the visual representation of it." I ask Buckle if it's playable anywhere, and the answer is, sadly, no. He still has the project files, but was unable to properly export it out of Unreal at the time, and probably won't be able to upload it anywhere because of all the copyrighted elements it uses.
Working on Nights Bridge, Buckle became interested in the linear nature of film as it evolved over the years from black-and-white to colour and CGI, and the way we approach technology in deliberate stylistic decisions. "There's a kind of understanding now of if I were to make a film in black-and-white tomorrow, you're not going to think, oh, you couldn't afford to do it in color. You're going to think, you've chosen to do this in black-and-white," he says. "I think with video games, there's still this place where if you see an 8-bit game come out or you see something that's got PS1 graphics, the assumption probably is, oh, it's an indie game, they're a small team or something. So I was thinking, how can you make something where they might still have that assumption, but it is justified by the narrative of the game, or the concept of the game?"
There's something wonderfully intangible about Buckle's mashups, not simply because they're fun and speak intimately to extremely online followings of cult artists, but because of real thought given to the original vision and technical parameters of each medium and the periods they came from. For instance, Buckle's clip of Fellini's 1973 film Amarcord, reimagined as a late 90s/early 2000s isometric game, taps into the dreamy, surreal quality of the film while going a step further to infuse its atmosphere with the slice-of-life comedy and eccentricities associated with a specific era of adventure games (I'm looking at you, Prague chapters of Microids' Still Life); Fellini films are, if anything, the perfect period playground to unleash the best and brightest NPC behaviors imaginable, and have arguably inspired many an artist concerned with animating the minutiae of a living, breathing world.
"I'm drawn to films they would never make a video game of," Buckle says. "It's quite frustrating because you think, someone owns the rights to this, and this would never be allowed to happen… it's a shame that there isn't the kind of space for that." There have, of course, been several video game versions of story tropes that we hold dear: Rear Window was based on a story by Cornell Woolrich (writing as "William Irish") who made his name doing the kind of pulpy detective fiction, in the company of Raymond Chandler et al, that molded the entire stylistic trajectory of modern murder mysteries and the detective genre.
(If there was ever a licensed Rear Window game, I know in my heart of hearts that it would probably be shit, because of the way modern game development sacrifices every good idea to gormless businesspeople funding the work. There was, in fact, a Vertigo video game, which was crushingly mid, namely because you simply cannot expect tightly-directed, industry-defining art from a bygone era, produced during markedly different circumstances, to survive the explosive clown car of bad compromises, corporate malfeasance, and cruel mismanagement that currently define both the film and game industries.)
The thing, then, that I love most about Miles Buckle's Instagram, is the intense yearning and wishful thinking it triggers in me. There will never be a world where we will get the Amarcord game, nor do I truly want one, because it would close that powerfully magical gap between reality and fantasy. I would rather continue thinking about how perfect it would be, roaming the streets of the titular town with its weird little inhabitants all trying to survive Mussolini's Italy. There is something singularly powerful about an imaginary game that can only exist in the ether of one's mind, and while I share that overwhelming "I would love to play these games for real" sentiment that many of Buckle's followers express, I don't know if the world would, or should, let them be made.
Of course, if there was a chance that one of these games could be made, Buckle should be the person to do it. He would, if given the freedom and budget, love to make an adaptation of a film ("maybe Hitchcock or Fellini"). But right now, he's been wrapped in doing videos inspired by the 2005 Mattel toy, Pixel Chix, a Tamagotchi-meets-Polly Pocket sort of handheld dollhouse with dot-matrix LCD elements. It originated from a Japanese Sega gadget called 24H Pictohouse – a sort of interactive house-shaped alarm clock that eventually morphed into a life simulation toy featuring a digital "Gal" to take care of.
"If you just took the concept, making a video game that's sort of an apartment building, of these little windows of people…some sort of mystery game, I think could be quite cool," says Buckle. "Because I'm also really interested [in the Pixel Chix toy], the relationship between the screen and the physical set behind it and how some parts of it are real. So there'll be someone in a bed and you can see the duvet is part of the LCD… and then the bed frame, let's say, is a plastic mold. I'd quite like to do something where there's a mechanic where you have to interact with that environment, but some bits are fixed and some bits are digital." He has, of course, already tested some of this idea out using a scene from Billy Wilder's The Apartment (1960).
"When the technology is so quick… there's these little periods of time that don't get explored enough because a new console comes along or a new idea becomes really popular, so everyone's trying to do that thing," says Buckle when we discuss the recurring popularity of handcrafted games, or games made with older forms of technology. "So I don't even necessarily think it's just nostalgia… I think that certain genres of games – or maybe more art styles of games – should be returned to because they didn't get the full scope of what their potential was."

item.title: Wardogs, the new tactical shooter from Derby-based studio Bulkhead, has sold more than a million copies and passed 350,000 concurrent players within hours of launching into Steam early access. Read more
item.description:
Wardogs, the new tactical shooter from Derby-based studio Bulkhead, has sold more than a million copies and passed 350,000 concurrent players within hours of launching into Steam early access.
As IGN reports, the game's server queues filled up quickly as a result, with plenty of players unable to jump straight into a match due to server congestion.
"To cross a million copies sold as we launch into early access is mental," said Bulkhead CEO Joe Brammer. "We've spent the last few months showing people exactly what Wardogs is, what it isn't, and at one point literally gave everyone ten reasons not to buy it. We didn't want people buying into blind hype."
He continued: "So seeing more than one million people choose to jump in and play the game at early access launch means a huge amount to all of us. But this is still early access. We've got things to fix, things we want to improve, and a lot more we want to build. The best thing players can do now is keep playing, keep telling us what they think and keep giving us those ridiculous Wardogs moments."
Wardogs' matches put up to 100 players into three-way fights for control points, mixing tactical shooting with vehicle combat, base construction, and destructible terrain.
The game is currently PC-only through Steam, priced at £36.99, with Bulkhead confirming PS5 and Xbox versions are coming in 2028, though without a firm release date.
Bulkhead has said it expects interest to settle down over time, given the studio is planning a slower drip of content updates rather than trying to sustain launch-day numbers indefinitely.
For more, check out our original coverage of the early access announcement, including Bulkhead's now-infamous "10 Reasons NOT to Buy" pre-order trailer here.

item.title: Nintendo's new Legend of Zelda 40th anniversary Switch 2 sold out within hours of preorders opening, and scalpers are already scalping, with dozens of orders popping up on eBay for close to double its retail price. Read more
item.description:
Nintendo's new Legend of Zelda 40th anniversary Switch 2 sold out within hours of preorders opening, and scalpers are already scalping, with dozens of orders popping up on eBay for close to double its retail price.
Nintendo announced a new Zelda-themed console earlier this week, with Link-green Joy-Cons and a triangular pattern inspired by the golden glow of the Triforce. Plus, there's a similarly styled Switch 2 Pro Controller and carry case coming, too.
Retailers listed the console for preorder at around £435, £15 more than the standard Switch 2. All sold out almost immediately and Nintendo hasn't yet made the special edition available for preorder through its own store, nor said anything about restocking it before launch.
As GamesRadar+ reports, scalpers have since listed the console on eBay for anywhere between $700 and $985 (that's £520-£730ish). Some listings bundle it with the upcoming Ocarina of Time remake, even though Nintendo isn't offering any such bundle.
The Zelda-themed Switch 2 launches on 29th October, a week ahead of the Ocarina of Time remake itself, which arrives on 5th November.
You can see everything else revealed in the same Direct, including the Ocarina of Time remake itself, in Eurogamer's full roundup: everything announced at the Legend of Zelda 40th anniversary Nintendo Direct.
